games.title: Air, Sea, Soil or All Three? A card game of where things are found
games.context: This is a card game about what air, sea water and soil hold. Each card is spoken by a substance. You say whether it belongs to the air, the sea, the soil or all three.

setup.art: Twenty cards in a shuffled pile on a table, with four small tokens marked Air, Sea, Soil and All three in front of each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud while another player slides one token forward, face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads the front. Everyone else puts down one token, face down.

setup.art: The tokens turned face up and the reader showing the back of the card.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over. The reader reads the back.

printables.title: 20 clue cards: a substance speaks on the front, and its place and the reason are on the back

items.f: I am nitrogen. Here I am 78 parts in every 100.
items.b: Air. Nitrogen is the largest part of air, because it reacts with very few things.

items.f: I am argon, a gas that reacts with nothing. Here I am nearly 1 part in 100.
items.b: Air. Argon was found in air in 1894.

items.f: I am common salt, dissolved. A litre here holds about 30 grams of me.
items.b: Sea. Common salt is most of the 35 grams of salts in a litre of sea water.

items.f: I am a bitter magnesium salt, dissolved in water.
items.b: Sea. Magnesium salts make sea water taste bitter as well as salty.

items.f: I am humus, the dark remains of dead leaves and animals.
items.b: Soil. Microbes make humus as they break down dead plants and animals.

items.f: I am clay, the finest grains of broken rock. I am sticky when wet.
items.b: Soil. Sand, silt and clay are the mineral grains of soil.

items.f: I am water.
items.b: All three. Air holds water vapour, the sea is mostly water, and soil holds water in its gaps.

items.f: I am carbon dioxide.
items.b: All three. I am 4 parts in 10,000 of air. I dissolve in the sea, and roots and microbes breathe me out in soil.

items.f: I am oxygen.
items.b: All three. I am 21 parts in 100 of air. Fish breathe me dissolved in the sea, and roots breathe me in the gaps of soil.

items.f: I am ozone. I stop harmful light from the Sun.
items.b: Air. A thin layer of ozone lies high in the air.

items.f: I am soot from a diesel engine, floating.
items.b: Air. Soot and dust float in air and settle slowly on leaves, walls and lungs.

items.f: I am sulfur dioxide, fresh from a coal chimney.
items.b: Air. In a few days I turn into sulfuric acid and fall in rain.

items.f: I am calcium, about to be built into a coral's skeleton.
items.b: Sea. Corals, clams and snails take calcium out of sea water.

items.f: I am a grain of sand, a tiny piece of quartz.
items.b: Soil. A beach is sand too, but sand is a solid grain and is not dissolved in the sea.

items.f: I am water vapour, a gas nobody can see.
items.b: Air. Water vapour makes up from almost nothing to 4 parts in 100 of air.

items.f: I am red iron oxide, the same substance as rust.
items.b: Soil. Iron oxide colours the red laterite soil of Kerala and the Konkan coast.

items.f: I am a microbe.
items.b: All three. Microbes float in air, fill the sea and crowd the soil.

items.f: I am sodium. Rain washed me out of rock long ago, and I have stayed for millions of years.
items.b: Sea. Sodium is one half of common salt. It stays in the sea a very long time.

items.f: I am potassium, held on a crumb of clay until a root takes me.
items.b: Soil. Clay and humus hold food for roots, so that rain does not wash the food away.

items.f: I am nitrogen. A bacterium on a bean root has just caught me.
items.b: Soil. Some soil bacteria turn nitrogen from the soil's air into plant food.

printables.title: 4 place tokens: Air, Sea, Soil, All three. Print one set for each player

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader keeps the back hidden.
Every other player puts one place token face down. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader reads the back. Every player whose token matches the place on the back scores 1 point.
A player who also gives a reason scores 1 more point. The reader decides, using the back of the card.
With two players, swap the reader's role after every card. The reader does not guess on their own card.
Playing alone? Read a card, say the place aloud, then turn the card over. Score 1 point for each right place.
After all 20 cards, the player with the most points wins. If you play alone, your score out of 20 is your result.

flow.do: Cut out the 20 cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile. Give each player one set of four tokens.
flow.say: Each card is spoken by something found in air, in the sea or in soil. Some things are found in all three. Your four tokens are your four answers.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take four tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Air, Sea, Soil or All Three. You set up the cards and the tokens.

flow.do: Play the first ten cards. After each card, read the back aloud. Ask the question below after card five.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Choose a token and put it face down. Now turn it over. The reader reads the back. Who scored?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Pick a place token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: How did you decide where the card belongs?
good: I asked whether it is a gas, something dissolved, or a solid grain.
A share out of 100 told me it was the air.
Dissolved salts belong to the sea.

flow.parent: For a stuck child, ask: is it a gas, is it dissolved in water, or is it a solid grain? One child can play alone or with you.
flow.context: In this step of Air, Sea, Soil or All Three you play the first ten clue cards.

flow.do: Play the last ten cards the same way. Keep the score on a piece of paper.
flow.say: Ten more cards. This time, also try to say why. A good reason earns one more point.
flow.kid: Play ten more cards. Give a reason for each place.
flow.context: In this step of Air, Sea, Soil or All Three you play the last ten cards and give reasons.

flow.do: Count the points. Then sort all 20 cards into four heaps: Air, Sea, Soil and All three. Look at the All three heap together.
flow.say: Sort the cards into four heaps. Look at the heap for all three. What do those four things have in common?
flow.kid: Sort the cards into four heaps. Look at the All three heap.

check.q: Which of these is found in air, in sea water and in soil?
check.why: Air holds water vapour, the sea is mostly water and soil holds water in its gaps. Argon is a gas of the air, and humus is part of soil. Water, oxygen, carbon dioxide and microbes move between all three.

flow.context: This is the last step of Air, Sea, Soil or All Three. You sort the cards and look at what air, sea and soil share.

games.title: Clean Drop: reach the lake with the least acid
games.context: This is a board game about acid rain. You are a drop of water travelling from a cloud to a lake. You pick up acid from smoke on the way, and lose it on limestone.

setup.art: A board of 24 numbered squares in a winding path from a cloud at the top to a lake at the bottom, with a dice, two buttons as counters and a small bowl of dal grains.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the board. Put a counter on square 1. Put 20 grains of dal in a bowl. They are the acid.

setup.art: A child moving a button along the path and taking two dal grains from the bowl on a square that shows a chimney.
setup.caption: 2. Roll the dice and move. Take acid grains or give them back, as the square says.

setup.art: Two children at the lake square counting the dal grains in their hands.
setup.caption: 3. At the lake, count your grains. The drop with the least acid wins.

printables.title: 24 squares, from the cloud to the lake
items: 1. Start. You are a drop of water in a cloud over the sea. You carry no acid.
3. Question square. Take a question card.
4. A coal power station with no scrubber. Take 2 acid grains.
5. A busy city road. Take 1 acid grain.
7. A power station with a scrubber. The sulfur is caught. Move on 1 square.
8. Question square. Take a question card.
11. A lightning storm. Take 1 acid grain.
12. You fall as rain. From here on you are on the ground.
13. A dusty plain. The dust neutralises some acid. Give back 1 grain.
14. A granite hill. Granite does not neutralise acid. Nothing happens.
15. Question square. Take a question card.
16. A marble statue. The marble uses up 1 grain of your acid, and loses a little of its surface. Give back 1 grain.
17. A limestone hill. Limestone neutralises acid. Give back 2 grains.
18. A pine forest on thin soil. Your acid washes plant food out of the soil. Nothing changes for you.
19. Question square. Take a question card.
20. A field where the farmer has spread lime. Give back 1 grain.
21. A stream over granite. Nothing happens.
22. Question square. Take a question card.
23. People have spread powdered limestone at the lake's edge. Give back 1 grain.
24. The lake. Stop here and count your acid grains.

printables.title: 12 question cards: a question on the front, the answer on the back

items.f: Which gas from burning coal makes most acid rain?
items.b: Sulfur dioxide.

items.f: Clean rain is a weak acid. Which gas from the air makes it so?
items.b: Carbon dioxide.

items.f: Which is more acid: rain of pH 4 or rain of pH 5?
items.b: Rain of pH 4. A lower number means more acid.

items.f: Which rock neutralises acid: granite or limestone?
items.b: Limestone.

items.f: What does a scrubber on a power station catch?
items.b: Sulfur dioxide, before it leaves the chimney.

items.f: Name one thing that acid rain harms.
items.b: Any one of these: fish in lakes, soil, forests, marble or limestone buildings.

items.f: True or false: acid rain always falls close to the chimney that made it.
items.b: False. Wind can carry the gases hundreds of kilometres.

items.f: What do people spread on a sour lake to neutralise the acid?
items.b: Powdered limestone, also called lime.

items.f: Name one natural source of the gases that make rain acid.
items.b: A volcano, or lightning.

items.f: What colour is red cabbage water in an acid?
items.b: Pink.

items.f: Why did taller chimneys not solve acid rain?
items.b: The gases still went into the air and fell somewhere else.

items.f: Marble and limestone are the same substance. What is its name?
items.b: Calcium carbonate.

rules: You need the board, one dice, and a button or coin for each player. Put 20 grains of dal in a bowl. The grains are acid.
Every player starts on square 1 with no grains. Take turns to roll the dice and move that many squares.
Do what your square says. To take acid, take grains from the bowl. To give back acid, return grains to the bowl. If you have none to give back, nothing happens.
On a question square, another player reads you a question card. If you answer correctly, give back 1 grain. If you play alone, answer aloud and then turn the card over.
Twice in the game you may say 'Wind!' after a roll. Then you ignore that roll and roll again. You must take the second roll.
You do not need an exact roll to reach the lake. Stop on square 24 and wait for the others.
When everyone has reached the lake, count the grains. The player with the fewest grains wins. Playing alone? Try to reach the lake with 2 grains or fewer.

flow.do: Lay out the board. Put the dal grains in a bowl and shuffle the question cards. Read the rules aloud together.
flow.say: You are a drop of water in a cloud. You will travel through air and over land to a lake. Each grain of dal is acid. Try to reach the lake carrying as little as you can.
flow.kid: Lay out the board. Put your counter on square 1. Read the rules.
flow.context: This is the first step of Clean Drop. You set up the board, the acid grains and the question cards.

flow.do: Play the game by the rules until every player has reached the lake. Ask the question below when the first player passes square 12.
flow.say: Roll and move. Read your square aloud. Remember that you may call 'Wind!' twice, to roll again. When would that help you most?
flow.kid: Roll the dice and move. Read your square aloud. Take or give back grains.

ask.q: On which squares did drops pick up acid? What do those places have in common?
good: Places where coal or fuel burns.
The volcano and the lightning are natural sources.
The scrubber square gave no acid.

flow.parent: Square 12 is where the drop falls as rain. Before it, the squares are in the air. After it, they are on the ground.
flow.context: In this step of Clean Drop you play from the cloud to the lake. You take acid from smoke and lose it on limestone.

flow.do: Count each player's grains at the lake. Then talk about the squares that took acid away.
flow.say: Count your grains. Now look at the ground squares. Which ones took acid away from you? What rock or powder did the work?
flow.kid: Count your grains. Which squares took acid away? Why?

check.q: A drop of acid rain runs over a limestone hill. What happens to its acid?
check.why: Limestone reacts with acid and uses it up. This is why lakes on limestone stayed healthy. If you chose nothing happens, that is true of granite, which does not react with acid.

flow.parent: A lake that receives 4 or more grains from each drop would be too acid for young fish. The scrubber square shows the lasting answer: stop the gas before it leaves the chimney.
flow.context: This is the last step of Clean Drop. You count the acid each drop brought to the lake and look at what removed it.

experiments.title: Smoke in the Jar: which part of a match makes water sour?
experiments.question: When a match burns, do its gases make water acid? If they do, which part is the cause: the head of the match or the wooden stick?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Three jars will hold plain air, the gas from burning match heads and the gas from burning wood. In which jar will the indicator water turn pinkest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use three jars of the same size. Burn five match heads under jar B and five headless sticks under jar C, each for a count of three. Put 2 tablespoons of the same indicator water in every jar. Shake every jar 30 times. Only one thing changes: what burned under the jar.
results_table: Colour of the water after shaking

materials.item: clean, dry glass jars of the same size, with lids. Jam or pickle jars of 300 to 400 millilitres are right

indicator water. Chop a quarter of a small red cabbage. A grown-up boils it for 10 minutes in 2 tumblers of filtered or bottled drinking water. Cool it and strain it. It keeps for a week in the fridge. (No red cabbage? Soak the petals of 6 red hibiscus flowers in a tumbler of hot water for 15 minutes. The colour change is smaller.)
a box of safety matches with at least 12 matches, for the grown-up only
a candle or a diya, standing on a steel plate
a small bowl of water, to put out the matches
a tablespoon, scissors, a dry cotton cloth and a sheet of white paper

experiments.safety: A grown-up does every step with fire. Work on a steel plate, away from curtains and paper. Tie long hair back and keep a bowl of water ready. Open a window. Do not sniff the jars, because the gas from match heads stings the nose.
experiments.record: Draw a table with three rows, for jars A, B and C. Write what burned under each jar and the colour of the water after shaking.
experiments.context: In this experiment a grown-up burns match heads under one upturned jar and plain wood under another. Then you shake indicator water in each jar to see which gas makes water acid.

setup.art: Three empty glass jars labelled A, B and C on a table, beside a small jug of purple cabbage water, a lit candle on a steel plate and a bowl of water.
setup.caption: 1. Label three dry jars A, B and C. Jar A gets plain air only.

setup.art: A grown-up's hand holding a jar upside down with a cloth, and the other hand holding a flaring match just inside the jar's mouth, with a candle nearby.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up burns five match heads just inside upturned jar B, one at a time.

setup.art: The same grown-up holding a burning matchstick with no head just inside upturned jar C.
setup.caption: 3. The grown-up burns five sticks with no heads just inside upturned jar C.

setup.art: A child shaking a closed jar with a little coloured water in it, and two more jars standing on white paper.
setup.caption: 4. Put 2 tablespoons of indicator water in each jar. Shake 30 times. Compare the colours.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
cols: Colour of the water after shaking
rows: Purple, a little pinker than A

flow.do: Label three dry jars A, B and C. Show your child the purple indicator water. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: Jar A will hold plain air. Jar B will hold gas from burning match heads. Jar C will hold gas from burning wood. Then each jar gets indicator water. Which water will turn pinkest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three jars: plain air, match-head gas and wood gas. Which water turns pinkest? Why?

ask.q: What might a match head hold that the wooden stick does not?
good: Something that catches fire easily.
A chemical.
Sulfur, because of the sharp smell.

flow.parent: The indicator is pink in acid and purple in water that is neither acid nor base. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of Smoke in the Jar. You guess which gas will turn the indicator water pinkest.

flow.do: Your child pours 2 tablespoons of indicator water into jar A, closes the lid and shakes it 30 times. Stand jar A on the white paper.
flow.say: Jar A has only the air of this room. Pour in 2 tablespoons, close it and shake it 30 times. We will compare the other jars with this colour.
flow.kid: Pour 2 tablespoons into jar A. Close it. Shake it 30 times.

check.q: In Smoke in the Jar, why does jar A get no smoke?
options: To show the colour with plain air
Because jar A is the cleanest
check.why: Jar A is the control. Without it you could not tell whether the smoke or the shaking changed the colour. If you chose saving matches, remember that a fair test needs one jar where nothing is changed.

flow.context: In this step of Smoke in the Jar you shake indicator water in jar A, which holds plain air.

flow.do: Light the candle on the steel plate. Hold jar B upside down in one hand, with the dry cloth. Light a match at the candle with the other hand. At once hold the flaring head just inside the jar's mouth, for a count of three. Drop the match in the bowl of water. Do this with five matches. Then put the lid on while the jar is still upside down.
flow.say: I will do the fire. You count to three for each match, and you count the matches. The gas is hot, so it rises into the upturned jar. Do not sniff it.
flow.kid: A grown-up burns five match heads under jar B. Count to three each time.
flow.parent: Keep the jar's mouth pointing down the whole time, so that the warm gas stays inside. The glass gets warm, not hot. If a match goes out before the head flares, use another.
flow.context: In this step of Smoke in the Jar a grown-up burns five match heads just inside the upturned jar B.

flow.do: Turn jar B upright. Lift the lid a little, pour in 2 tablespoons of indicator water and close it quickly. Your child shakes it 30 times and stands it beside jar A.
flow.say: Now the water goes in. Shake it 30 times, so that the gas meets the water. Look at the colour against the white paper.
flow.kid: Shake jar B 30 times. Stand it beside jar A. Look at both colours.
flow.context: In this step of Smoke in the Jar you shake indicator water in jar B, with the match-head gas.

flow.do: Cut the heads off five matches with scissors, and drop the heads in the bowl of water. Hold jar C upside down. Light each headless stick at the candle. Hold its burning end just inside the jar for a count of three. Put the lid on. Then add 2 tablespoons of indicator water, and your child shakes the jar 30 times.
flow.say: Jar C gets burning wood with no match head. Everything else stays the same: five sticks, a count of three, 2 tablespoons and 30 shakes.
flow.kid: A grown-up burns five headless sticks under jar C. Then shake it 30 times.
flow.parent: A headless stick lights slowly. Hold it in the candle flame until it burns by itself. Blow out the candle when you finish.
flow.context: In this step of Smoke in the Jar a grown-up burns five headless matchsticks under jar C. Then you shake it.

flow.do: Stand the three jars in a row on the white paper, in good light. Your child writes each colour in the table. Ask them to say what they thought would happen, what they saw and why it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at the three colours. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. What does a match head give that plain wood does not?
flow.kid: Write the three colours. Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Coal holds sulfur, as a match head does. What might happen to rain that falls through the smoke of a coal power station?
good: The gas dissolves in the rain.
The rain becomes acid.
It is like jar B, but in the sky.

flow.parent: Most families find jar B clearly pinker than jar A. Jar C is the same as jar A, or a little pinker. Write down what you really see. The reason: a match head holds sulfur. Burning sulfur makes the gas sulfur dioxide, which dissolves in water and makes an acid. Burning wood makes carbon dioxide, which makes only a weak acid. If jar B did not change, your water may be hard, because hard water uses up acid. Make fresh indicator water with bottled drinking water and use eight matches.
flow.think: A match head is tiny. A power station burns thousands of tonnes of coal a day. Where does all its sulfur dioxide go?
flow.context: This is the last step of Smoke in the Jar. You compare the colours of jars A, B and C and explain them.

experiments.title: The Lemon Drop Test: which stones does acid mark?
experiments.question: Acid rain is sour water falling on buildings and statues. Which stones does a sour drop mark, and which does it leave unharmed?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. You will put a drop of lemon juice on marble, granite, a glazed tile, steel and a shell. Which of them will the lemon mark? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Put one drop of the same lemon juice on every surface. Put one drop of plain water beside it. Leave every drop for the same time, 10 minutes. Wipe every spot the same way and look at it under the same light. Only the surface changes.

materials.item: a lemon, cut in half (or 2 teaspoons of vinegar)
a piece of polished marble: an offcut from a tile shop, a broken marble tile, or the underside of a marble rolling board
a piece of polished granite: an offcut, or a hidden corner of a granite kitchen counter
an old glazed ceramic tile, plate or cup
a steel plate
a seashell or a piece of clean eggshell. If you have them, also a bit of kadappa stone, a piece of brick and a cement flower pot
a teaspoon, a dry cloth, a torch or a phone light, and a magnifying glass if you have one
slips of paper marked L for lemon and W for water, and a clock

experiments.safety: Lemon juice leaves a dull mark on polished marble that does not wipe off. Use an offcut, a broken piece or a hidden corner, and ask the owner first. Keep lemon juice away from your eyes.
experiments.record: Draw a table with one row for each surface. Write yes or no for bubbles, and yes or no for a mark after wiping.
experiments.context: In this experiment you put drops of lemon juice and of water on marble, granite and other surfaces. After 10 minutes you wipe them and look for a dull mark.

setup.art: A piece of white marble, a piece of dark speckled granite, a glazed tile, a steel plate and a seashell laid in a row on newspaper, with half a lemon beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the surfaces. Guess which ones the lemon will mark.

setup.art: A child's hand letting one drop of lemon juice fall from a teaspoon onto a marble piece, next to a drop of water and two paper slips marked L and W.
setup.caption: 2. Put one drop of lemon juice and one drop of water on each surface.

setup.art: A child looking through a magnifying glass at a drop on marble that has tiny bubbles in it.
setup.caption: 3. Look for tiny bubbles in each lemon drop while you wait 10 minutes.

setup.art: A child wiping the marble dry and shining a phone torch low across it, showing one dull round patch on the shiny surface.
setup.caption: 4. Wipe every spot dry. Shine a light low across it. Is there a dull mark?

flow.do: Lay the surfaces in a row on newspaper. Put the paper slips L and W beside each one. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: Lemon juice is an acid, much stronger than acid rain. Each surface gets one drop of lemon and one drop of water. Which surfaces will the lemon mark? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Each surface gets a lemon drop. Which ones will it mark? Why?

ask.q: Why do we also put a drop of plain water on each surface?
good: To see whether water alone leaves a mark.
Then we know the acid did it and not the wetness.

flow.parent: Many children expect the hardest-looking stone to be safe and the steel to be harmed. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Lemon Drop Test. You guess which surfaces a drop of lemon juice will mark.

flow.do: Your child squeezes lemon juice into the teaspoon. They put one drop beside each L slip and one drop of water beside each W slip. Note the time.
flow.say: One drop of lemon by each L. One drop of water by each W. Make the drops the same size. Now we start the clock for 10 minutes.
flow.kid: Put a lemon drop by each L. Put a water drop by each W.
flow.parent: A grown-up cuts the lemon. The rest your child can do.
flow.context: In this step of the Lemon Drop Test you put a lemon drop and a water drop on each surface.

flow.do: While you wait, your child looks closely at every lemon drop. A magnifying glass or a zoomed-in phone camera helps. They write yes or no for bubbles. Look again after 5 minutes.
flow.say: Look into each lemon drop. Can you see tiny bubbles growing on the stone under it? Look at the water drops too. Write yes or no for each surface.
flow.kid: Look closely at each lemon drop. Are there tiny bubbles? Write yes or no.

check.q: A lemon drop on marble makes tiny bubbles. What are the bubbles?
options: A new gas made by the acid and the marble
Air that was hiding in the lemon
check.why: The acid reacts with the marble and makes carbon dioxide gas. A new gas is a sign of a chemical reaction. If you chose air from the lemon, look at the lemon drop on granite: it has no bubbles.

flow.context: In this step of the Lemon Drop Test you watch the drops for 10 minutes and look for tiny bubbles.

flow.do: After 10 minutes your child wipes every spot dry with the cloth. They shine the torch low across each surface and look for a dull patch. They rub a fingertip over the spot. Write yes or no for a mark.
flow.say: Wipe each spot dry. Now shine the light low, almost flat along the surface. Is the shine the same where the lemon was? Rub the spot gently. Is it as smooth as before?
flow.kid: Wipe each spot dry. Shine the light low across it. Is there a dull mark?
flow.parent: The mark on polished marble is a dull round patch, seen best with the light coming from the side. A shell feels rough or chalky where the drop was.
flow.context: In this step of the Lemon Drop Test you wipe the drops away. Then you look for a dull mark with a low light.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw and why it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. What do the marked surfaces have in common?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: The Taj Mahal is marble. The Brihadisvara temple at Thanjavur is granite. Which one could acid rain mark?
good: The Taj Mahal, because marble reacts with acid.
The granite temple would hardly change.

flow.parent: Marble, shell, eggshell and kadappa stone are all calcium carbonate. Acid reacts with calcium carbonate, makes bubbles of carbon dioxide and dissolves a little of the surface. The spot turns rough, so it loses its shine. Cement and brick mortar react too. Granite is made of minerals that acid hardly touches. A glazed tile has a skin of glass, and steel plates are made to resist acid. So acid rain harms buildings and statues of marble and limestone most.
flow.think: Acid rain is far weaker than lemon juice. But it falls for a hundred years. What would it do to a marble carving?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Lemon Drop Test. You say which surfaces the lemon juice marked, and why.

experiments.title: Two Lakes: which lake bed neutralises acid rain?
experiments.question: Acid rain fell on thousands of lakes. Some lakes lost their fish, and others stayed healthy. Can the rock under a lake change what acid rain does to the water?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Two tumblers of water get the same sour rain. One has glass marbles at the bottom, and the other has crushed shell. Will both stay pink? Will one go back to purple? Which one, and why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use two tumblers of the same size, with the same amount of water and the same amount of indicator water. Add the same number of vinegar drops to each. Stir both for the same count. Only the lake bed changes: glass marbles in one, crushed shell in the other.

materials.item: clear glass tumblers of the same size

indicator water. Chop a quarter of a small red cabbage. A grown-up boils it for 10 minutes in 2 tumblers of filtered or bottled drinking water. Cool it and strain it. It keeps for a week in the fridge. (No red cabbage? Soak the petals of 6 red hibiscus flowers in a tumbler of hot water for 15 minutes. The colour change is smaller.) You need 4 tablespoons.
drinking water, 1 tumbler
for the limestone bed: the washed and dried shells of 2 eggs, or 3 small seashells, crushed to bits as small as rava
for the granite bed: 6 glass marbles, or a heaped teaspoon of washed dark pebbles
vinegar, 1 tablespoon, and a teaspoon to drip it from
two spoons for stirring, a clock, a sheet of white paper and two labels

schedule.what: Set up the two lakes, add the sour rain and record the colours for 20 minutes.
Look at both lakes again in the morning, and say what happened.

experiments.safety: Wash your hands after touching eggshells. A grown-up crushes the shells if they are sharp.
experiments.record: Draw a table with rows for these times: before the rain, just after the rain, 5 minutes, 10 minutes, 20 minutes and the next morning. Write the colour of each lake at each time.
experiments.context: In this experiment two tumblers are two small lakes. One has a bed of glass marbles, which stand for granite. The other has a bed of crushed shell, which stands for limestone. Both get the same sour rain.

setup.art: Two glass tumblers of purple water on white paper, one with glass marbles at the bottom labelled Lake Granite and one with white crushed shell at the bottom labelled Lake Limestone.
setup.caption: 1. Make two purple lakes. Put marbles in one and crushed shell in the other.

setup.art: A child dripping vinegar from a teaspoon into one of the tumblers, and both tumblers now pink.
setup.caption: 2. Add vinegar drop by drop to both lakes until both are pink. Count the drops.

setup.art: A child stirring both tumblers with two spoons beside a clock, with one tumbler still pink and the other turning purple.
setup.caption: 3. Stir both every 2 minutes. Write the colours after 5, 10 and 20 minutes.

setup.art: The two tumblers the next morning on a windowsill, one pink and one purple-blue.
setup.caption: 4. Look again the next morning.

flow.do: Crush the shells to bits as small as rava. Fold them in paper and roll a rolling pin over them. Half fill both tumblers with drinking water. Add 2 tablespoons of indicator water to each. Ask for the guess and the reason.
flow.say: These two tumblers are two lakes. One will lie on glass marbles, which stand for granite. The other will lie on crushed shell, which stands for limestone. Both will get the same sour rain. What will happen to each? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Two lakes get the same sour rain. What will happen to each? Why?
flow.parent: Shell, limestone and marble are the same substance, calcium carbonate. Glass is made from sand and reacts with acid as little as granite does. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Lakes. You make two purple lakes and guess what sour rain will do to each.

flow.do: Your child puts the 6 marbles into one tumbler and labels it Lake Granite. They put a heaped teaspoon of crushed shell into the other and label it Lake Limestone. Stir both. Write the colours in the first row.
flow.say: Marbles go into Lake Granite. Crushed shell goes into Lake Limestone. Stir both for a count of ten. Write the colour of each lake before the rain.
flow.kid: Put marbles in one lake. Put crushed shell in the other. Stir both.
flow.context: In this step of Two Lakes one lake gets a bed of glass marbles. The other gets a bed of crushed shell.

flow.do: Your child adds vinegar to both lakes, one drop to each in turn, and stirs. Stop when both lakes are clearly pink. Count the drops, which must be the same for both. Write the number and the colours.
flow.say: Now it rains acid. One drop in this lake, one drop in that lake, and stir. Go on until both are pink. Count the drops aloud.
flow.kid: Add vinegar to both lakes, drop by drop. Stop when both are pink.
flow.parent: Most water needs 5 to 15 drops. If yours needs many more, your water is hard. Hard water holds dissolved limestone from the ground, and that uses up the first drops of acid.
flow.context: In this step of Two Lakes you add the same number of vinegar drops to each lake. Both turn pink.

flow.do: Start the clock. Every 2 minutes your child stirs both lakes for a count of ten. They write the colours after 5, 10 and 20 minutes. Hold the white paper behind the tumblers to compare.
flow.say: Stir both lakes the same way, every 2 minutes. Look at them against the white paper. Is either lake changing? Write the colours each time.
flow.kid: Stir both lakes every 2 minutes. Write the colours after 5, 10 and 20 minutes.

check.q: In Two Lakes, why must both lakes get the same number of vinegar drops?
options: So that only the lake bed differs
So that the vinegar lasts longer
So that both lakes smell the same
check.why: A fair test changes one thing. If one lake got more acid, you could not tell whether the bed or the acid made the difference. If you chose another answer, ask yourself what the test is trying to compare.

flow.parent: Lake Limestone usually goes back towards purple within 10 to 30 minutes. Finer shell works faster. Lake Granite stays pink. If nothing has changed after 20 minutes, the shell bits are too big. Crush them finer and stir again.
flow.context: In this step of Two Lakes you stir both pink lakes for 20 minutes and record their colours.

flow.do: Add the same number of vinegar drops again to both lakes, as a second shower of acid rain. Stir and watch for 3 minutes. Then leave both tumblers where nobody will knock them.
flow.say: Here comes a second shower, with the same number of drops. Watch both lakes. Which one can cope with more acid rain? We will look again tomorrow morning.
flow.kid: Add the same drops again to both lakes. Watch. Leave them until morning.
flow.wait: Leave both tumblers overnight and look again in the morning
flow.context: In this step of Two Lakes you give both lakes a second shower of vinegar drops and leave them overnight.

flow.do: Next morning, your child writes the colour of each lake. Ask them to say what they thought would happen, what they saw and why it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at the two lakes. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Where did the acid in Lake Limestone go?
flow.kid: Write the two colours. Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: A real lake lies on granite and is turning acid. What could people add to help it?
good: Powdered limestone.
Crushed shells.
Something that neutralises acid.

ask.q: Would it be better to add limestone to the lake, or to stop the acid rain? Why?
good: Stop the acid rain, because the limestone gets used up.
Both: limestone helps now, and stopping the smoke helps for good.

flow.parent: The crushed shell is calcium carbonate. It reacted with the acid and used it up, so the water went back to purple. This is called neutralising. The glass marbles did not react, so Lake Granite stayed pink. Real lakes on limestone were protected in the same way. Lakes on granite in Sweden and Norway lost their fish. Sweden has spread powdered limestone on thousands of lakes.
flow.think: Each shower of acid uses up a little of the shell. What happens to a limestone lake if acid rain falls for 200 years?
flow.context: This is the last step of Two Lakes. You look at both lakes the next morning and explain the difference.

activities.title: A Bottle of Sea: mix sea water by its recipe

materials.item: a half-litre bottle of drinking water
table salt, 3 level teaspoons
a teaspoon
a small bowl of plain drinking water, to compare
a slip of paper and tape for a label

schedule.what: Guess how much salt the sea holds, mix a bottle of sea water by the recipe and taste one drop.

activities.safety: Taste one drop from a clean fingertip, and no more. Do not drink the bottle. Water as salty as the sea makes you thirstier and can make you sick.
activities.record: Write one sentence: how much salt you guessed, and how much the recipe needed.
activities.context: In this activity you make water as salty as the sea, using the real recipe. Then you taste one drop of it.

setup.art: A half-litre plastic bottle of water on a kitchen counter beside a steel salt box and a teaspoon.
setup.caption: 1. Take half a litre of drinking water. Guess how much salt the sea would have in it.

setup.art: A child tipping a level teaspoon of salt into the mouth of the bottle through a paper cone.
setup.caption: 2. Add 3 level teaspoons of salt. Close the bottle and shake until the water is clear.

setup.art: A child touching a wet fingertip to her tongue, with the labelled bottle and a bowl of plain water in front of her.
setup.caption: 3. Taste one drop from a fingertip. Then taste a drop of plain water.

flow.do: Put the bottle, the salt and the teaspoon on the table. Ask for the guess and the reason before any salt goes in.
flow.say: This bottle holds half a litre of water. How much salt would make it as salty as the sea? Show me with the spoon. Why do you think so?
flow.kid: How much salt makes this bottle as salty as the sea? Why?

ask.q: Have you ever tasted sea water? What was it like?
good: Very salty.
Salty and a bit bitter.
I have not, but people say you cannot drink it.

flow.parent: Most children guess a pinch or half a spoon. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Bottle of Sea. You guess how much salt is in half a litre of sea water.

flow.do: Your child adds 3 level teaspoons of salt to the bottle and closes it. They shake it until no grains are left. Stick on a label that says 'Bottle of Sea. Do not drink.' Your child tastes one drop from a clean fingertip, and then a drop of plain water.
flow.say: The sea's recipe is about 35 grams of salt in a litre. For half a litre that is 3 level teaspoons. Shake until the water is clear. Now taste one drop from your fingertip.
flow.kid: Add 3 level teaspoons of salt. Shake until clear. Taste one drop only.

check.q: The salt in the bottle can no longer be seen. Where is it?
options: Spread through the water in tiny particles
check.why: The salt has dissolved. Its particles are spread through the water, too small to see, and you can still taste them. If you chose the air or changed into water, taste the drop again: the salt is still there.

flow.parent: A level teaspoon of fine salt weighs about 6 grams, so 3 teaspoons are about 18 grams. Real sea water also holds a little magnesium salt, which makes it taste bitter as well as salty.
flow.context: In this step of A Bottle of Sea you add 3 level teaspoons of salt to the water. Then you taste one drop.

flow.do: Sit together. Ask your child to say what they guessed and what the recipe needed. Then ask the question below, and leave it open.
flow.say: Say what you guessed, and what the recipe needed. Now think about this. River water has no salty taste, and every river runs into the sea. So where could the sea's salt come from?
flow.kid: Say what you guessed and what you found. Where could the sea's salt come from?

ask.q: Where could the salt in the sea come from?
good: From rocks under the sea.
Maybe rivers bring a little.
I do not know yet.

flow.parent: Do not give the answer. The Plate That Got Saltier tests one idea over five days. Pour the Bottle of Sea down the sink afterwards. Do not water plants with it.
flow.context: This is the last step of A Bottle of Sea. You compare your guess with the recipe and ask where the sea's salt comes from.

activities.title: One Hundred Grains of Air: count out the recipe of air

materials.item: raw rice, 78 grains
toor dal or chana dal, 21 grains
mustard seeds, 2
a steel plate
a sheet of paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Guess how much of the air is oxygen, then count out 100 grains that stand for the gases in air.

activities.record: Draw the plate. Write how many grains stand for nitrogen, oxygen and argon.
activities.context: In this activity you count out 100 grains to stand for the gases in air. Rice is nitrogen, dal is oxygen and one mustard seed is argon.

setup.art: Rice grains laid out on a sheet of paper in neat rows of ten, with a child's finger counting them.
setup.caption: 1. Count 78 grains of rice in rows of ten. They stand for nitrogen.

setup.art: Two rows of yellow dal and one more grain beside the rows of rice, and a single mustard seed.
setup.caption: 2. Count 21 grains of dal for oxygen. Add 1 mustard seed for argon.

setup.art: A steel plate holding the mixed rice, dal and one mustard seed, with a second mustard seed lying outside the plate.
setup.caption: 3. Mix all 100 on a plate. This is air. Carbon dioxide is too rare to be on the plate.

flow.do: Ask the question below before any counting. Write down the guess and the reason.
flow.say: Air is a mixture of gases. Suppose the air in this room were 100 grains. How many of them would be oxygen, the gas we need? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The air is 100 grains. How many are oxygen? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Which gases do you think are in air?
good: Oxygen.
Carbon dioxide.
Nitrogen.
Water vapour.

flow.parent: Many children say that air is mostly oxygen, or half oxygen and half carbon dioxide. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of One Hundred Grains of Air. You guess how many grains out of 100 stand for oxygen.

flow.do: Your child counts 78 grains of rice in rows of ten, then 21 grains of dal. They add 1 mustard seed. Check that the total is 100. Mix them on the plate.
flow.say: Rice is nitrogen. Count 78 grains, in rows of ten. Dal is oxygen. Count 21. One mustard seed is argon. That makes 100. Now mix them. This plate is the air.
flow.kid: Count 78 rice, 21 dal and 1 mustard seed. Mix them on the plate.

check.q: Which gas makes up most of the air?
check.why: Nitrogen is 78 parts in every 100. Oxygen is 21 parts. If you chose oxygen, that is a common idea, because oxygen is the gas we talk about most. Carbon dioxide is far less than 1 part in 100.

flow.parent: Rows of ten make the counting easy to check: seven full rows and 8 more for rice, two rows and 1 more for dal.
flow.context: In this step of One Hundred Grains of Air you count out 100 grains of rice, dal and mustard. Then you mix them.

flow.do: Put the second mustard seed on the table, outside the plate. Explain the carbon dioxide number. Then ask your child to say what they guessed and what they found.
flow.say: Where is the carbon dioxide? Only about 4 grains in 10,000 are carbon dioxide. You would need 25 plates like this one to hold a single grain of it. Say what you guessed about oxygen, and what you found.
flow.kid: Carbon dioxide is 1 grain in 25 plates. Say what you guessed and found.

ask.q: With every breath you take in 78 parts of nitrogen. What do you think your body does with it?
good: Nothing. It breathes it out again.
It does not use it.

ask.q: Carbon dioxide is so rare in air. Why might it still matter?
good: Plants make their food from it.
It dissolves in rain.
It keeps the Earth warm.

flow.parent: Your body breathes the nitrogen out again unchanged. Plants build their bodies from carbon dioxide, and it also makes rain slightly acid. Keep the paper with the counts for Hundred Squares.
flow.think: Nitrogen reacts with almost nothing. Could that be why so much of it is in the air?
flow.context: This is the last step of One Hundred Grains of Air. You find out how rare carbon dioxide is, and compare your guess with the plate.

activities.title: Hundred Squares: draw the recipes of sea water and soil

materials.item: squared paper, or plain paper and a ruler to draw two grids of 10 squares by 10 squares
colour pencils or crayons: blue, brown, black and yellow
a pencil

schedule.what: Guess the shares, then colour one grid of 100 squares for sea water and one for good garden soil.

activities.record: Keep the two coloured grids. Write the key beside each one.
activities.context: In this activity you colour two grids of 100 squares. One shows what sea water is made of, and the other shows what good garden soil is made of.

setup.art: Two empty grids of ten squares by ten squares drawn on paper, one labelled Sea water and one labelled Soil.
setup.caption: 1. Draw two grids of 100 squares. Guess how many squares will be salt, and how many will be air.

setup.art: A grid with almost every square coloured blue, and three and a half squares in one corner coloured yellow.
setup.caption: 2. Sea water: colour 3 and a half squares yellow for salts. Colour the rest blue for water.

setup.art: A grid with 45 brown squares, 25 blue squares, 25 empty squares and 5 black squares.
setup.caption: 3. Soil: 45 brown for minerals, 25 blue for water, 25 empty for air and 5 black for humus.

flow.do: Draw the two grids, or mark them on squared paper. Ask both questions below and write down the guesses.
flow.say: Each grid has 100 squares. In the sea water grid, how many squares do you think are salt? In the soil grid, how many are air? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: How many squares of sea water are salt? How many squares of soil are air?
flow.parent: Many children guess that a quarter of sea water is salt and that soil has no air at all. Do not correct the guesses.
flow.context: This is the first step of Hundred Squares. You guess how much of sea water is salt and how much of soil is air.

flow.do: Your child colours 3 and a half squares yellow, in one corner of the sea water grid. They colour the other 96 and a half squares blue. Then they put a dot on 3 of the yellow squares.
flow.say: Sea water is 3 and a half parts salts in every 100. Colour those yellow. Colour the rest blue for water. The 3 dotted squares are common salt. The last half square is all the other salts.
flow.kid: Colour 3 and a half squares yellow for salts. Colour the rest blue.
flow.parent: The half square stands for the bitter salts of magnesium and a few others. They are why sea salt from the pans is purified before it is sold.
flow.context: In this step of Hundred Squares you colour the sea water grid: 3 and a half squares of salts and the rest water.

flow.do: On the soil grid your child colours 45 squares brown, 25 blue and 5 black. They leave 25 squares empty and write 'air' across them.
flow.say: Good garden soil has four parts. Colour 45 squares brown for mineral grains. Colour 25 blue for water and 5 black for humus. Leave 25 empty. Those are air.
flow.kid: Colour 45 brown, 25 blue and 5 black. Leave 25 empty for air.

check.q: In good garden soil, about how much is water and air together?
check.why: 25 squares are water and 25 are air, which makes 50 out of 100. If you chose almost none, think of water soaking into a flower pot: it goes into the gaps between the grains.

flow.context: In this step of Hundred Squares you colour the soil grid: minerals, water, humus and air.

flow.do: Lay the two grids side by side. If you did One Hundred Grains of Air, put that drawing beside them. Ask your child to say what they guessed and what they found.
flow.say: Say what you guessed and what you found. Now look for water. Is there water in sea water, in soil and in air?
flow.kid: Say what you guessed and found. Which of the three recipes hold water?

ask.q: Which of the three mixtures hold water?
good: All three.
Sea water is mostly water, soil holds water in its gaps, and air holds water vapour.

flow.parent: In One Hundred Grains of Air, 78 grains of rice stood for nitrogen and 21 grains of dal for oxygen. That plate showed dry air. Real air also holds up to 4 parts in 100 of water vapour.
flow.context: This is the last step of Hundred Squares. You compare the recipes of sea water, soil and air.

projects.title: The Plate That Got Saltier: can fresh-tasting water make something salty?

materials.item: a one-litre bottle of filtered or bottled drinking water
table salt: one small pinch, as much as a thumb and one finger can hold
a wide steel plate with a rim, clean and dry
a tablespoon
a sunny windowsill or balcony
a thin cloth or a wire sieve, to keep dust and insects off the plate
a notebook page and a pencil

projects.safety: Taste one drop from a clean fingertip, and no more. If dust, a bird dropping or an insect has landed on the plate, do not taste. Look at the white film instead.

schedule.what: Mix the river water, taste it, write your guess and pour the first 4 tablespoons on the plate.
Check that the plate is dry, and pour on 4 more tablespoons of river water.
Check that the plate is dry, and pour on 4 more tablespoons of river water.
Check that the plate is dry, and pour on 4 more tablespoons of river water.
Check that the plate is dry, and pour on the last 4 tablespoons of river water.
Add 1 tablespoon of plain water to the dry plate, taste one drop and say what happened.

projects.record: Each day, write the day and whether the plate was dry. On day 1 and day 6, write what one drop tasted like.
projects.context: In this six-day project a plate is a small sea. Each day you pour on a little 'river water' that tastes fresh, and the sun dries it. On the last day you taste the plate.

setup.art: A child dropping a small pinch of salt into a one-litre bottle of water labelled River water.
setup.caption: 1. Dissolve one small pinch of salt in a litre of water. This is the river water. It should taste fresh.

setup.art: A wide steel plate on a sunny windowsill with a thin layer of water on it, and a tablespoon beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Pour 4 tablespoons onto the plate each day for 5 days. Let the sun dry it each time.

setup.art: The same plate, dry, with a faint white film on the steel, and a child adding one tablespoon of water to it.
setup.caption: 3. On day 6, add 1 tablespoon of plain water to the dry plate and swirl it.

setup.art: A child touching a fingertip to the plate and then to her tongue, with the river water bottle beside her.
setup.caption: 4. Taste one drop from the plate. Then taste one drop of the river water.

flow.do: Day 1. Your child drops one small pinch of salt into the litre of water and shakes it. They taste one drop. It should taste like plain water. If it tastes salty, pour out half and fill the bottle up again. Label it 'River water'. Ask for the guess and the reason. Then pour 4 tablespoons onto the plate and set it in the sun.
flow.say: A real river holds a tiny amount of dissolved rock, too little to taste. This bottle is our river. Each day we pour 4 tablespoons onto the plate, and the sun dries it. On day 6, will the plate taste salty? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Taste the river water. Pour 4 tablespoons on the plate. Will the plate get salty? Why?

ask.q: When the sun dries the plate, where will the water go? Where will the salt go?
good: The water goes into the air.
The salt stays on the plate.
Maybe the salt goes with the water.

flow.parent: A thin layer dries within a day on a sunny sill. In damp monsoon weather, pour only 2 tablespoons a day and count the total at the end. Cover the plate with a thin cloth or a sieve if there is dust.
flow.context: This is day 1 of The Plate That Got Saltier. You make river water that tastes fresh, guess, and pour the first 4 tablespoons on a plate.

flow.do: Days 2 to 5. Once a day, your child checks that the plate is dry. Then they pour 4 more tablespoons of river water onto the same plate. Do not wipe the plate. Keep the bottle closed.
flow.say: Is the plate dry? Where did yesterday's water go? Where is yesterday's salt? Pour on 4 more tablespoons. The river keeps running.
flow.kid: Is the plate dry? Pour on 4 more tablespoons. Do not wipe the plate.
flow.wait: Do this once a day for four days

ask.q: The plate has had water poured on it for days. Why is it not full?
good: The water evaporated.
The sun took the water into the air.

flow.parent: If the plate is still wet, move it to a sunnier place and wait a few hours. A faint white film may show by day 3 or 4.
flow.context: These are days 2 to 5 of The Plate That Got Saltier. Each day you pour 4 more tablespoons of fresh-tasting river water onto the same plate.

flow.do: Day 6. Look at the dry plate in good light. Your child adds 1 tablespoon of plain drinking water and swirls it over the whole plate with a clean finger. They taste one drop. Then they taste one drop from the river bottle. Ask them to say what they thought would happen, what they found and why it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Add 1 tablespoon of plain water and swirl it everywhere. Taste one drop. Now taste a drop of the river water. Say what you thought would happen, what you found, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Add 1 tablespoon of water. Swirl and taste one drop. Say what you found and why.

check.q: In The Plate That Got Saltier, water was poured on for five days. Why did the plate never fill up?
options: The salt soaked up the water
check.why: The sun turned the water into vapour, which went into the air. The salt cannot evaporate, so it stayed. If you chose the salt soaking it up, remember how little salt there was: one pinch in a whole litre.

ask.q: Rivers have run into the sea for billions of years. How is the sea like your plate?
good: Rivers bring a little salt and the sun takes only the water.
The salt builds up because it has no way out.

flow.parent: Twenty tablespoons of river water went onto the plate. All their salt is now in 1 tablespoon. So the drop is about 20 times as salty as the river water. The sea works the same way. Rivers bring a little dissolved rock, and water leaves the sea only by evaporating. One difference matters. Salt also leaves the real sea slowly, buried in mud and in beds of rock salt. So the sea's saltiness now stays about the same.
flow.think: A lake with a river flowing out of it stays fresh. Why?
flow.context: This is day 6 of The Plate That Got Saltier. You taste the plate after five days of fresh-tasting river water, and explain the result.

challenges.title: The Rain Catcher: collect rain with nothing else in it
challenges.problem: Scientists who study acid rain must collect rain and nothing else. Dust, leaves, bird droppings and water splashing up from the ground all change the result. Build a rain catcher for a balcony or a window ledge. It must catch falling water, keep dust out before the rain starts, block splashes and stand firm in wind.
constraints: Rain test: a helper pours one mug of water slowly through a colander held an arm's length above. Your catcher must collect at least 4 tablespoons.
Dust test: before the rain test, sprinkle a pinch of turmeric powder over the catcher. The water you collect must not be yellow.
Splash test: pour half a mug of water on the floor right beside the catcher, from knee height. No splashed water may get in.
Wind test: the catcher must stay standing when you push it gently three times with one finger.
Use only things from home. You may open or move a lid by hand when the rain starts.
materials: a plastic bottle of 1 or 2 litres
a second plastic bottle, whose top a grown-up cuts off to make a funnel
a steel bowl or mug, a small plate and a colander or sieve
string, sticky tape, rubber bands and a few clean stones
an upturned bucket or a stool to stand the catcher on
a pinch of turmeric powder, a tablespoon and a mug of water
general: Stand a funnel in the mouth of a bottle, so that a wide opening feeds a narrow neck.
Put clean stones in the bottom of the bottle so that the wind does not tip it.
Raise the catcher on an upturned bucket, above the height that splashes reach.
Cover the funnel with a small plate, and lift the plate off when the rain starts.
creative: Tie the lid to a string, so that you can pull it off from indoors without getting wet.
Fit a paper or plastic collar around the funnel, sloping outwards like a small roof, to throw splashes off.
Rest a clean marble in the funnel. Water runs in around the marble, and less dust falls in afterwards.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own rain catcher. It must pass all four tests: the rain test, the dust test, the splash test and the wind test. Draw your design and write which test was hardest to pass. On a rainy day, catch real rain with it. Put 2 tablespoons of the rain in a glass. Add 1 tablespoon of indicator water, which is the red cabbage water of Smoke in the Jar. Do the same with tap water, and compare the colours.
challenges.context: In this challenge you build a catcher that collects falling rain and keeps out dust and splashes. It is the problem scientists had to solve before they could measure acid rain.

flow.do: Read the problem together. First let your child try the plainest catcher, a steel bowl on the floor. Run the dust test, the rain test and the splash test on it.
flow.say: Start with a plain bowl on the floor. Sprinkle the turmeric, pour the rain and splash the floor beside it. What got into the bowl that was not rain?
flow.kid: Test a plain bowl on the floor. What gets in that is not rain?

ask.q: What got into the bowl besides the rain?
good: The turmeric dust.
Water that splashed up from the floor.
It would also catch leaves and insects.

flow.parent: Do this in a bathroom or on a balcony, because the floor gets wet.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Rain Catcher. You test a plain bowl on the floor and find what goes wrong.

flow.do: Your child chooses a plan and builds it. A grown-up cuts the top off a bottle to make a funnel, if one is needed.
flow.say: Choose your plan and build it. How will you keep dust out before the rain? How will you keep splashes out? What will stop it falling over?
flow.kid: Choose a plan and build it. A grown-up cuts the bottle.
flow.parent: Cover the cut edge of the bottle with tape, because it is sharp.
flow.context: In this step of the Rain Catcher you build your own design from bottles, stones, string and a lid.

flow.do: Run the four tests in this order: dust, rain, splash and wind. After the rain test, measure the water with the tablespoon and look at its colour. Record each test as pass or fail.
flow.say: Now we test. Sprinkle the turmeric with the lid on. Take the lid off and pour the rain. Splash the floor. Push three times. How many tablespoons did you catch? Is the water yellow?
flow.kid: Run the four tests. Count the tablespoons. Is the water yellow?
flow.context: In this step of the Rain Catcher you run the dust, rain, splash and wind tests on your design.

flow.do: Your child changes one thing to pass a failed test, or to catch more water. Test again. Then talk about the question below.
flow.say: Which test was hardest? Change one thing and test again. You took the lid off by hand. How could a catcher know by itself that rain has started?
flow.kid: Which test failed? Change one thing. Test again.

ask.q: Why does a little dust in the catcher matter so much to a scientist measuring acid rain?
good: Dust can neutralise the acid.
Then the water is not only rain, so the pH is wrong.

flow.parent: Scientists use a catcher with a lid moved by a small motor. A sensor feels the first drops and opens the lid, and it closes the lid when the rain stops. Praise a clear account of what failed as much as a pass.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Rain Catcher. You improve your design and compare it with the catchers scientists use.

worksheets.title: Three recipes and a sour rain

items.p: Out of 100 parts of dry air, how many are nitrogen?
items.why: Nitrogen is 78 parts in every 100. Oxygen is 21 parts, and argon is nearly 1 part.

items.p: A litre of sea water holds about ____ grams of dissolved salts.
items.why: Sea water is about 3 and a half parts salts in every 100. That is about 35 grams in a litre.

items.p: Clean rain is pure water with a pH of exactly 7.
items.why: False. Carbon dioxide from the air dissolves in rain and makes a weak acid. Clean rain has a pH of about 5.6.

items.p: Match each mixture to its largest part.
items.why: Each mixture has one part that is far bigger than the rest. Air is mostly nitrogen, sea water is mostly water, and soil is mostly grains of broken rock.

items.p: Sort these sources of acid gases. Is each one natural, or made by people?
items.why: Volcanoes give out sulfur dioxide, and lightning makes nitrogen oxides. Most of the extra acid in rain today comes from burning coal and fuel.

items.p: What is humus?
opts: The dark remains of dead plants and animals
items.why: Microbes break down dead leaves, roots and animals, and humus is what is left. It is dark and holds water well.

items.p: Put these in order, to show how a coal fire far away harms a lake.
items: Coal burns in a power station
Sulfur dioxide rises from the chimney
Wind carries the gas far away
The gas turns into acid in a cloud
Acid rain falls on a lake
a: Coal burns in a power station
Sulfur dioxide rises from the chimney
Wind carries the gas far away
The gas turns into acid in a cloud
Acid rain falls on a lake
items.why: The sulfur in coal becomes sulfur dioxide gas. Wind carries it, it turns into acid in the cloud, and the acid falls in rain.

items.p: Which of these does acid rain damage most?
items.why: Marble is calcium carbonate, which reacts with acid and dissolves. Granite, glass and glazed tiles hardly react.

items.p: Acid rain always falls close to the chimney that made it.
items.why: False. Wind can carry the gases for hundreds of kilometres before they fall, sometimes into another country.

items.p: Using up an acid with limestone or a base is called ____ the acid.
items.why: Limestone reacts with an acid and uses it up. The water is then no longer acid.

items.p: In The Plate That Got Saltier, each day's water tasted fresh. Why did the plate taste salty on day 6?
items.a: The river water held a very small amount of salt. Each day the water evaporated and the salt stayed on the plate. After five days the salt of 20 tablespoons was all in one place.
items.why: A strong answer says that the water left and the salt stayed, and that small amounts added up.

items.p: In Smoke in the Jar, the match-head jar turned pinkest. What does that tell you about coal smoke and rain?
items.a: Match heads hold sulfur, and burning sulfur makes a gas that turns water acid. Coal holds sulfur too. So the smoke of burning coal can make rain acid.
items.why: A strong answer links sulfur in the match head to sulfur in coal, and the jar of water to rain.

items.p: Draw rain on a hill, a river, the sea and vapour rising. Show with dots where the salt goes.
items.a: Rain falls on a hill. A river with a few dots runs to the sea. The sea is full of dots. Arrows of vapour rise from the sea with no dots in them, and go back to the cloud.
items.why: A strong drawing shows dots going into the sea with the river and none leaving with the vapour.
items.art: A blank box with a hill on the left and a wavy line for the sea on the right.

items.p: A factory's smoke is making the town's air dirty. What should be done?

views.says: Build a taller chimney. It costs less, and it sends the smoke high above the town.

views.who: A fish farmer by a lake 300 kilometres away
views.says: The smoke does not vanish. It falls on my lake as acid rain, and my young fish die.
Fit a scrubber. It costs more, but it catches the sulfur before it leaves the chimney.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from what you know about acid rain. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that the gases travel hundreds of kilometres, so a tall chimney only moves the harm. Another is that a scrubber costs money that someone has to pay.
items.why: Each speaker has a real point. A strong answer uses a fact about how the gases travel or how a scrubber works.

items.p: Why is a lake with no river flowing out usually salty?
opts: Salts arrive and only water leaves
Salt falls into it with the rain
Its bed is always made of salt
items.why: Rivers bring a little dissolved rock. Water leaves such a lake only by evaporating, and the salts stay behind and build up.

worksheets.title: Follow the gas, follow the salt

items.p: You breathe in air with 78 parts nitrogen. What does your body do with the nitrogen?
items.why: Nitrogen reacts with very few things. Your body breathes it out again, still 78 parts in 100.

items.p: One rain has a pH of 4.6. Clean rain has a pH of 5.6. How do they compare?
opts: The first is 10 times as acid
The first is slightly more acid
The clean rain is more acid
items.why: Each whole step down the pH scale means 10 times more acid. From 5.6 to 4.6 is one whole step.

items.p: Sea water is an acid.
items.why: False. Sea water is slightly basic, with a pH of about 8. Dissolved carbon dioxide is making it a little less basic.

items.p: Every ocean has the same recipe of salts, even though some seas are saltier than others.
items.why: True. Samples from every ocean have the salts in the same proportions. This shows that the oceans keep mixing.

items.p: Three of these are calcium carbonate. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Marble, seashell and limestone are all calcium carbonate, which reacts with acid. Granite is made of other minerals that hardly react.

items.p: Sort these. Is most of each one found in air, in the sea or in soil?
items.why: Argon and ozone are gases of the air. Sodium and magnesium are dissolved in the sea. Humus and clay are solid parts of soil.

items.p: A litre of sea water holds 35 grams of salts. How many grams do 4 litres hold?
items.why: 35 grams in each litre, for 4 litres, is 35 times 4, which is 140 grams.

items.p: Put these waters in order, from the least salty to the most salty.
items.why: Rain holds almost no salts. River water has dissolved a little rock. The sea has kept its salts for ages. The Dead Sea has no way out and a hot sun.

items.p: The slow breaking of rock by rain, air and living beings is called ____.
items.why: Rain is a weak acid. Over thousands of years it dissolves part of the rock, and what stays behind becomes soil.

items.p: Why does crushed shell turn sour pink water back to purple?
opts: It reacts with the acid, using it up
It soaks up the pink colour
items.why: Shell is calcium carbonate. It reacts with the acid, so less acid is left and the indicator goes back to purple.

items.p: In the Lemon Drop Test, marble was marked and granite was not. Explain why, using the words calcium carbonate.
items.a: Marble is calcium carbonate. Acid reacts with calcium carbonate and makes bubbles of gas. It dissolves a little of the surface, so the shine is lost. Granite is made of minerals that acid hardly touches.
items.why: A strong answer names what marble is made of and says the acid reacted with it. It also says that granite did not react.

items.p: A lake has rivers flowing in and one river flowing out. Explain why its water stays fresh.
items.a: The rivers bring a little dissolved rock. The river flowing out carries the same salts away again. So the salts do not build up.
items.why: A strong answer says that the salts have a way out. It may compare this with the sea, where only water leaves.

items.p: Carbon dioxide is only 4 parts in 10,000 of air. Give two reasons why it still matters.
items.a: Plants build their bodies from it. It dissolves in rain and makes rain a weak acid, which slowly breaks rock into soil. It also dissolves in the sea and helps to keep the Earth warm.
items.why: A strong answer gives any two real jobs of carbon dioxide. A small share can still do a great deal.

items.p: Label four parts of this magnified view of soil.
a: A mineral grain: a piece of broken rock, such as a grain of sand
Humus: a dark crumb made from dead plants and animals
Water: a thin film around the grains
An air gap: an empty-looking space between the grains
items.why: Soil has four parts. About half of good soil is grains and humus. The other half is the water and air in the gaps.
items.art: A magnified view of soil with pale grains, dark crumbs, a blue film around the grains and white gaps, with four blank label lines.

items.p: India's air often carries a lot of dust from dry soil. Is this dust good or bad?

views.says: It is bad. Fine dust goes deep into the lungs and makes children cough.
It helps. The dust is rich in calcium, and it neutralises acid in the rain.

views.who: A person who looks after old monuments
views.says: It is bad. Dust and soot stick to marble and turn it yellow and brown.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then say what one of the others has right.
items.a: Any view with a reason. A strong answer sees that the same dust harms lungs and marble and also protects lakes. So the answer depends on what you are trying to protect.
items.why: All three speakers are right about what they study. A strong answer weighs the harm against the help.

items.p: Nitrogen taken from air weighed slightly more than nitrogen made from chemicals. What explained the difference?
opts: An unknown heavier gas in the air
items.why: The nitrogen from air held a little argon, which is heavier. A small difference that keeps coming back is a clue, not a mistake.

items.p: A lake on granite is turning acid. Which action stops the cause?
items.why: A scrubber stops the gas that makes the acid. Limestone helps the lake for a time, but it is used up while the acid rain goes on.

items.p: Which test would show that fresh-tasting river water holds dissolved minerals?
opts: Dry a plateful and look for a film
Look at it through a magnifier
Shake it hard in a bottle
items.why: Dissolved minerals are too small to see and too few to taste. When the water evaporates they stay behind as a faint film.

items.p: As the air gains carbon dioxide, sea water becomes less basic. Why?
opts: The gas dissolves and makes a weak acid
items.why: Carbon dioxide dissolves in the sea, as it does in a raindrop, and makes carbonic acid. The pH of the sea surface has fallen from about 8.2 to 8.1.

items.p: The sea gets saltier every year.
items.why: False. Rivers add salts, but salts also leave the sea slowly. They are buried in mud and in beds of rock salt. So the saltiness stays about the same.

items.p: Most of the oxygen in the air was made by living beings.
items.why: True. Plants, algae and some bacteria make oxygen from water, using sunlight. Without them the oxygen would slowly react with rocks and be used up.

items.p: Match each problem to an answer that people really use.
pairs: Sulfur dioxide from a power station
A lake that is already acid
items.why: The first three stop the gases before they reach the air. Limestone treats the harm after it has happened.

items.p: The salt from 20 tablespoons of river water is dissolved in 1 tablespoon. How many times as salty is it?
items.why: The same salt is now in one twentieth of the water. So each drop holds 20 times as much salt.

items.p: A lake with no river flowing out loses its water only by ____.
items.why: Only water evaporates. The salts stay, so such a lake turns salty over time.

items.p: Living beings add oxygen and carbon dioxide all day. Why is nitrogen still the largest part of air?
items.a: Nitrogen reacts with very few things, so it is hardly ever used up. It stays in the air for millions of years. Oxygen and carbon dioxide are used up almost as fast as they are made.
items.why: A strong answer says that the share of a gas depends on how long the gas stays in the air.

items.p: Taller chimneys made the air in towns cleaner. Explain why they did not solve acid rain.
items.a: A tall chimney only sends the gases higher. The wind carries them further, and they still turn into acid and fall in rain somewhere else.
items.why: A strong answer says that the gases were moved and not removed.

items.p: A match-head jar in Smoke in the Jar stayed purple. Give one reason other than 'smoke makes no acid'.
items.a: The water may have been hard, and hard water uses up a little acid. Or too few matches were used, or the gas escaped before the lid went on.
items.why: A strong answer looks for a fault in the test before throwing away an idea that other tests support.

items.p: Rock salt is mined from hills far from any sea. What does that tell you about those hills?
items.a: The salt was left when a sea or a salt lake dried up long ago. Later the salt beds were buried and lifted into hills. So that land was once under salt water.
items.why: A strong answer reasons from the rule that salt stays when water evaporates.

items.p: The sea's water is replaced every few thousand years. Its salt stays for millions of years. What is the sea?

views.says: The sea is the water. Take the water away and only a dry bed of salt is left.
The sea is the salt. The water keeps leaving, and the salt is what stays.
The sea is neither part alone. It is water and salts arriving and leaving at different speeds.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. A strong answer uses the fact that water leaves by evaporating and salt stays. It says what that means for which part is 'the sea'.
items.why: This question has no single right answer. A strong answer uses how long each part stays.

items.p: Draw a power station, a cloud and a lake. Show how acid rain forms, and one way to stop it.
items.a: Smoke rises from the chimney. An arrow of wind carries it to a cloud, and rain falls on the lake. The change could be a scrubber on the chimney, cleaner fuel, or power made without burning coal.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the gas travelling before it falls. It puts the change at the source, not at the lake.
items.art: A blank box with a small power station on the left and a lake on the right.

quiz.p: Which list gives the three main gases of dry air, largest first?
quiz.why: Dry air is 78 parts nitrogen, 21 parts oxygen and nearly 1 part argon. Carbon dioxide is far less than 1 part.

quiz.p: About how much of the air is carbon dioxide?
quiz.why: Carbon dioxide is rare in air. Breathed-out air holds about 4 parts in 100, which may be why many people choose that number.

quiz.p: What is most of the salt in sea water?
opts: Common salt, the salt we eat
quiz.why: About 85 grams in every 100 grams of sea salt are common salt, sodium chloride.

quiz.p: Rivers taste fresh. How do they still make the sea salty?
opts: They bring a little dissolved rock
They wash salt off the beaches
They freeze and leave salt behind
They do not. Fish make the salt
quiz.why: River water holds a very small amount of dissolved rock. It adds up, because the salts stay in the sea when the water evaporates.

quiz.p: When sea water evaporates, what goes into the air?
opts: The water and the salt together
quiz.why: Water turns into vapour and rises. Salt cannot evaporate in the sun, so it stays. That is how a salt pan works.

quiz.p: Which four parts make up soil?
quiz.why: Soil is mineral grains, humus, water and air. About half of good soil is the water and air in the gaps.

quiz.p: Why is clean rain slightly acid?
opts: Salt from the sea rises into it
All dust in the air is acid
quiz.why: A raindrop falls through air and dissolves a little carbon dioxide, which makes a weak acid. Salt does not rise with the vapour.

quiz.p: Which two kinds of gas cause most acid rain?
quiz.why: Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides turn into strong acids in clouds. Carbon dioxide makes only the weak acid of clean rain.

quiz.p: Gases from a chimney in one country can fall as acid rain in another country.
quiz.why: True. Wind carries the gases for hundreds of kilometres. Smoke from other countries in Europe fell as acid rain on Sweden and Norway.

quiz.p: Two lakes get the same acid rain. Which lake stays healthier?
quiz.why: Limestone reacts with the acid and neutralises it. Granite does not, so a lake on granite turns acid.

quiz.p: What does acid rain do to a marble carving over many years?
opts: Dissolves the surface and blurs it
quiz.why: Acid reacts with the calcium carbonate of marble and dissolves a little each time. Sharp edges slowly become blurred.

quiz.p: What is the lasting way to stop acid rain?
opts: Stop the gases at the chimney
quiz.why: Scrubbers and cleaner fuel stop the gases from reaching the air. Taller chimneys only move the acid, and limestone is used up.

applications: Salt makers along the coasts of Gujarat and Tamil Nadu let sea water into shallow pans. The sun evaporates the water, and they rake up the salt.
Scrubbers on power stations spray limestone into the smoke to catch sulfur dioxide. The gypsum that is left is made into wall boards.
Oil companies take sulfur out of petrol and diesel, so that engines give out far less sulfur dioxide.
Farmers test the pH of their soil. If it is too acid, they spread lime, which is powdered limestone, to neutralise it.
Factories cool air until it turns to liquid, and then separate it. Hospitals use the oxygen, food packers use the nitrogen and welders use the argon.
Chennai makes drinking water from sea water at plants in Minjur and Nemmeli. They push the water through very fine filters that hold back the salts.
Scientists around the world collect rain and measure its pH every week. The records show where acid rain is growing and where it is shrinking.
