open_questions.q: Where did the Earth's water come from?
open_questions.why_open: The water in some meteorites matches sea water well, and the water in one comet did not. But only a few comets and meteorites have been measured, and the young Earth's own rock may have held enough.

open_questions.q: How salty was the sea when it first formed?
open_questions.why_open: No sea water that old survives. Scientists study tiny drops trapped in ancient salt crystals. The oldest of these cover only part of the Earth's history.

open_questions.q: How will shell builders cope as the sea becomes less basic?
open_questions.why_open: In tanks, some corals and snails build thinner shells in such water, and some seem to manage. Nobody knows yet what will happen in the open sea over many years.

open_questions.q: What has kept the oxygen in air close to 21 parts in 100 for millions of years?
open_questions.why_open: Plants make oxygen, and burning and rotting use it up. Scientists have several ideas about what keeps the two in balance, such as forest fires, and they do not agree.

open_questions.q: How long do soils take to recover from acid rain?
open_questions.why_open: In some forests the rain has been cleaner for 30 years, and the soil is still short of calcium. New calcium comes only from the slow weathering of rock.

open_questions.q: Is anything alive in the acid clouds of Venus?
open_questions.why_open: In 2020 a team reported a gas called phosphine there, which living beings can make. Other teams could not find it. The question is still argued.

ask_kids: You just breathed in. Most of that breath was nitrogen. Where is that nitrogen now?
Is there any salt in the water you are drinking? How could you find out without tasting it?
Look at a puddle drying on the road. What goes up, and what stays behind?
If our town built a very tall chimney, who would get the smoke?
Which things in our home are marble, and which are granite? How could you tell?
Why do you think tears and sweat taste salty?
Soil looks solid. What is in the gaps between its grains?
It is raining. What has this rain picked up on its way down?

jokes.j: Why did the salt stay in the sea?
jokes.a: Because the sun only offered the water a lift.

jokes.j: What did the raindrop say to the smoke?
jokes.a: Stay away. You make me sour.

jokes.j: Why does argon never join a reaction?
jokes.a: It is asked every time. It just never feels like it.

jokes.j: What did the marble say to the lemon?
jokes.a: You take the shine off everything.

jokes.j: Why was the river so proud?
jokes.a: It had delivered salt for a million years and never missed a day.
Seventy-eight. It talks about nothing else.

jokes.j: Why did the limestone lake stay calm in the acid rain?
jokes.a: It had an answer for every sour remark.

jokes.j: What did the soil say to the air?
jokes.a: Come in. A quarter of me is yours.

jokes.j: Why did the cloud leave the salt behind?
jokes.a: It never picked it up in the first place.

maths.problem: In The Plate That Got Saltier, you poured 4 tablespoons of river water on the plate each day. You did this for 5 days. On day 6 you dissolved all the salt in 1 tablespoon of water. How many times as salty as river water was that tablespoon?
maths.explain: 4 tablespoons a day for 5 days is 4 × 5 = 20 tablespoons. All the salt from 20 tablespoons is now in 1 tablespoon. So each drop holds 20 times as much salt as a drop of river water.
maths.context: In The Plate That Got Saltier you dry fresh-tasting 'river water' on a plate every day. You taste the plate at the end.
maths.why_maths: The dry plate looks almost empty. Multiplying shows how much river water its salt came from.

maths.problem: In One Hundred Grains of Air, 100 grains stood for air: 78 of rice, 21 of dal and 1 mustard seed. You want a bigger model with 500 grains. How many grains of rice, of dal and of mustard do you need?
maths.answer: 390 grains of rice, 105 grains of dal and 5 mustard seeds.
maths.explain: 500 is 5 times 100, so every share is 5 times as big. 78 × 5 = 390, 21 × 5 = 105 and 1 × 5 = 5. Check: 390 + 105 + 5 = 500.
maths.context: In One Hundred Grains of Air you count rice for nitrogen, dal for oxygen and a mustard seed for argon.
maths.why_maths: A recipe keeps the same shares at any size. Scaling it up shows that air has the same recipe in a room or over a whole country.

maths.problem: About 4 parts in every 10,000 parts of air are carbon dioxide. How many grains would a model of air need, to hold just 1 grain of carbon dioxide? How many plates of 100 grains is that?
maths.answer: 2,500 grains, which is 25 plates of 100 grains.
maths.explain: 10,000 ÷ 4 = 2,500. So 4 grains in 10,000 is the same share as 1 grain in 2,500. And 2,500 ÷ 100 = 25 plates.
maths.context: In One Hundred Grains of Air, the plate of 100 grains had no grain for carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide is too rare for that.
maths.why_maths: A share as small as 4 in 10,000 is hard to picture. Dividing turns it into a number of plates you can picture on a table.

maths.problem: The sea holds about 35 grams of salts in a litre. In A Bottle of Sea you put 3 level teaspoons of salt into half a litre of water. A level teaspoon holds about 6 grams. Was your bottle more salty or less salty than the sea?
maths.answer: Very slightly more salty: 18 grams, where the sea would have 17 and a half grams.
maths.explain: Half a litre of sea water holds half of 35 grams, which is 17 and a half grams. 3 teaspoons of 6 grams are 18 grams. The difference is only half a gram, so the recipe is close enough.
maths.context: In A Bottle of Sea you mix half a litre of water as salty as the sea, using teaspoons.
maths.why_maths: A teaspoon is a rough measure. Working out the grams shows whether a kitchen recipe is close to the real one.

maths.problem: Each whole step down the pH scale means 10 times more acid. Clean rain has a pH of about 5.6. How many times as acid as clean rain is a rain of pH 3.6?
maths.explain: From 5.6 down to 3.6 is two whole steps. One step is 10 times, and two steps are 10 × 10 = 100 times.
maths.context: In Smoke in the Jar, gas from burning match heads turns water acid. The smoke of burning coal turns rain acid in the same way. The pH scale measures how acid a liquid is.
maths.why_maths: On the pH scale a small change in the number is a large change in the acid. Multiplying by ten for each step shows how large.

maths.problem: In Two Lakes, one family crushed their shell as fine as rava, and Lake Limestone turned purple in 10 minutes. Another family used the same weight of shell in big pieces, and it took 40 minutes. How many times as long did the big pieces take? What could explain it?
maths.answer: 4 times as long. Fine bits have far more surface touching the water.
maths.explain: 40 ÷ 10 = 4. The acid can only react at the surface of the shell. The same shell crushed finer has much more surface, so it uses up the acid faster.
maths.context: In Two Lakes, crushed shell at the bottom of a tumbler neutralises sour water. The water turns from pink back to purple. These two results are made up.
maths.why_maths: Saying 'four times as long' makes an odd result stand out. Then you look for its cause.

odd: Nitrogen, oxygen and argon are gases in air, but humus is a part of soil.
Marble, limestone and seashell are calcium carbonate and react with acid, but granite does not.
A power station, a lorry and a kiln burn fuel and give out acid gases, but a windmill burns nothing.
Sand, clay and humus are parts of soil, but salt spray comes from the sea.
Rain, river water and tap water are fresh, but sea water holds 35 grams of salts in a litre.

how_we_found_out.story: For a hundred years, chemists were sure they knew what air was made of. It was nitrogen and oxygen, with a little carbon dioxide and water vapour. One clue did not fit. In 1785 Henry Cavendish used electric sparks to make the nitrogen and oxygen of air react, again and again. A small bubble of gas was always left over, and nothing would make it react. He wrote this down, and almost everyone forgot it. In the 1890s Lord Rayleigh weighed gases with great care. Nitrogen taken from air was always a little heavier than nitrogen made from chemicals. The difference was about one part in 200. Many people would have blamed the scales. Rayleigh and the chemist William Ramsay looked for the cause instead. They removed the oxygen and then the nitrogen from a sample of air. A heavier gas was left, and it would not react with anything. In 1894 they named it argon, from a Greek word meaning lazy. Nearly 1 part in every 100 parts of air is argon. It had been in every breath anyone had ever taken.
how_we_found_out.who: Henry Cavendish, Lord Rayleigh (John William Strutt) and William Ramsay, all in Britain
how_we_found_out.when: Cavendish found his leftover bubble in 1785. Rayleigh and Ramsay announced argon in 1894.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That air was only nitrogen and oxygen, with a little carbon dioxide and water vapour. Rayleigh showed that nitrogen from air was heavier than pure nitrogen. With Ramsay he then separated the extra gas, argon.

roots.context: In this unit you found what air, sea water and soil are made of. You also found why the sea keeps its salt. Here we ask what it means that some things stay and others pass through.

deep_truth.truth: In The Plate That Got Saltier, each day's water tasted fresh, yet the plate ended up salty. The water left for the air every day, and the salt stayed. The sea keeps its salt the same way, and the air keeps nitrogen, which hardly reacts. So what a place is made of depends on what stays there, as well as on what arrives.
deep_truth.habit: We expect a place to be made mostly of whatever is poured into it most. Rivers pour far more fresh water than salt into the sea, yet the sea is salty. What stays longest builds up.
deep_truth.evidence: In The Plate That Got Saltier, 20 tablespoons of fresh-tasting water left one salty plate. A lake with a river flowing out stays fresh. A lake with no way out, such as Sambhar Lake, turns salty. Argon reacts with nothing and has built up to nearly 1 part in 100 of air.

three.who_am_i: The calcium in your bones was once in rock. Rain dissolved that calcium, and it reached you through your food. It has stayed in you. The nitrogen in your last breath did not stay: you breathed it out unchanged.
three.what_is_life: Living beings change the recipes around them. The oxygen in air is there only because plants, algae and bacteria keep making oxygen. Humus is the part of soil that living beings made.
three.what_is_this_world: Air, sea and soil keep passing things to each other. A gas from the air dissolves in rain. Rain dissolves rock. Rivers carry the dissolved rock to the sea, and the sea's water rises into the air again.

roots.thread: Air, sea water and soil look like three separate things. But the water of the sea was once vapour in the air. The salt of the sea was once rock in a hill. The clay in a field is what rain left when it carried the rest away. Each of the three is being made, all the time, out of the other two. Many sages taught that the world is one whole that appears as many things. The science here says something close and plain: you can name three recipes, but the ingredients keep moving between them.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka asks his son Shvetaketu to put a lump of salt in water. The next morning the salt cannot be seen or picked out. But every sip, from the top, the middle and the bottom, tastes of salt.
teachings.link: This is A Bottle of Sea. The salt is still there after it dissolves, spread through all the water. Uddalaka uses it to point at something unseen that is present in everything. The dissolving is science, and what he points to is a teaching.

teachings.teaching: The rivers of the east flow east and the rivers of the west flow west. They rise from the sea and go back to the sea, and become the sea. There they do not know 'I am this river' or 'I am that river'.
teachings.link: The verse describes the water cycle: the sea's water rises, falls as rain and returns by the rivers. In the sea, the water of the Kaveri and of the Ganga cannot be told apart. The verse uses this to speak about the self, which science does not test.

teachings.teaching: All the rivers run into the sea, yet the sea is not full. To the place where the rivers come from, there they return again.
teachings.link: This is the cousin's puzzle in the story The Oldest Salt Pan, noticed more than 2,000 years ago. The sea does not fill up because water leaves it as vapour. The writer saw the pattern, and evaporation explains it.

science.text: In all this dissolving, evaporating and raining, no atom is made or lost. The sodium in the sea today is the same sodium that rain once washed out of rock.

In 1974 James Lovelock and Lynn Margulis proposed that living beings keep the air and the sea steady. They called this one system Gaia. Scientists agree that life changes the air and the sea. They do not agree that life steers them.

other_view.who: The Buddha's teaching of anicca, which means impermanence
other_view.view: Nothing stays. The salt of the sea is buried in time, lifted into hills as rock salt and washed back by rain. Even the nitrogen of the air is slowly caught by bacteria and lightning. On this view, 'what stays' only means what leaves slowly. A place is not made of anything fixed. It is only a pattern of arriving and leaving.

practice.title: Five breaths and a glass of water
practice.say: Sit with a glass of drinking water in front of you. Breathe in slowly and out slowly, five times. Each breath in is mostly nitrogen, which you will give back unchanged. Each breath out carries a little water from your body into the room. Now take one sip. This water has been rain, river and sea many times. Sit quietly for a moment and notice what is passing through you and what is staying.
practice.kid: Sit with a glass of water. Breathe in and out slowly, five times. Each breath out carries a little water away. Take one sip. This water was once rain and sea. Notice what passes through you.

ask: In The Plate That Got Saltier, the water left the plate and the salt stayed. In you, what passes through and what stays?
The water of the sea is replaced every few thousand years, and the salt stays for millions. Is it the same sea?
You breathed out nitrogen exactly as you breathed it in. Was that nitrogen ever part of you?

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game and challenge was reasoned through step by step. It was read as a parent and child in a city flat would do it. None has been tried at home yet, so treat the expected results as likely, not certain. A Bottle of Sea needs only salt and water. One Hundred Grains of Air needs rice, dal and a mustard seed. The Plate That Got Saltier takes six days and a sunny sill. It works because the water evaporates and the salt cannot. In damp monsoon weather the plate dries slowly, and the step says to pour less each day. Do not taste the plate if dust has landed on the plate, or an insect has. Smoke in the Jar needs a grown-up for every step with fire, and it needs red cabbage water. The colour change is clearest in soft water. Hard tap water uses up some of the acid. So the indicator should be made with filtered or bottled water. The last step says what to do if nothing changes. The Lemon Drop Test is the surest result in the unit, because lemon juice always dulls polished marble. That mark does not come off, so use an offcut or a hidden corner. Polished granite, glazed tile and steel should show no mark in 10 minutes. Two Lakes works only if the shell is crushed as fine as rava. Bigger pieces react too slowly to see in 20 minutes. Vegetarian families can use seashells in place of eggshells. One batch of red cabbage water, kept in the fridge, serves both indicator experiments for about a week. Red hibiscus petals are offered in its place, but their colour change is smaller and has not been checked. The Rain Catcher is tested with a mug and a colander, so it does not need a rainy day. Clean Drop and the card game can each be played alone. No part needs a garden. Facts were checked on 17 Nov 2026 against NOAA, NASA, the US EPA, the Supreme Court order, the journals and the other sources listed. Softened: which countries sent the acid rain to Sweden and Norway, how many salt pans Thoothukudi has, Tamil Nadu's rank among salt states, and when the Marakkanam pans can be seen. The shares of air are for dry air and are rounded. The soil recipe of 45, 25, 25 and 5 is the usual textbook figure, and real soils vary widely. The sea's 35 grams in a litre is an average. The times that water and salt stay in the sea are estimates. The three videos have no address yet.
